h: A generation across borders: the young are asking to see the bill for what they inherit
dek: In The Wire, Shelley Walia writes that the students who walked out of classes across Europe on 20 November are not just angry: they are asking why they should pay the price of war, debt and a heating planet, and young Indians are asking the same question.
body: Shelley Walia, a former professor at Panjab University, begins with the moment on Friday, 20 November, when students in London, Amsterdam and many other cities walked out of their classes at the same time. More than 50 student and youth groups called the strike under the slogan 'Fight for our future, not their wars', and it spread to more than 25 countries. For the writer, the new thing is not the anger. It is that this generation is speaking together across borders.

Education, housing, rising prices, climate and the arms race: Walia ties all these grievances to one question, which is where governments spend public money. He recalls Eisenhower's 1953 remark that the cost of one bomber could build brick schools in more than thirty cities. In Germany there is opposition to the return of military conscription, and the demands also include solidarity with Palestinians.

He recalls Paris in 1968, when the fire that started at the Sorbonne reached the factories and nearly ten million workers brought France to a halt, and then Soweto in 1976. But those revolts stayed inside their own countries, while today the arms trade, the climate crisis and speculative capital all move across borders.

The writer warns that in many countries dissent is now treated as a law and order problem. Students face surveillance and police batons, and people who oppose war are called foreign agents. Intellectuals are silent while nineteen-year-olds are speaking up. But success depends on alliances with teachers, unions and farmers, as the Punjab farmers who camped at Delhi's borders showed.

In India he remembers students in the freedom struggle and in the resistance to the Emergency, and those who marched towards Parliament this summer against the discredited exam system. Their question was the same: why should we pay for decisions others make? In his view the real test is whether budgets, syllabuses and laws actually change.
nazar: In India, protests by young people are often dismissed as 'sedition' or a 'foreign conspiracy', exactly as the writer sees happening in Europe. The questions of a generation struggling with exam scams, unemployment and costly education are fair, and they must be met with answers, not with lathis (police batons).

The most useful point is the one about alliances. The farmers' movement showed that when different groups come together, those in power have to bend. If students stand with workers, farmers and teachers, their voice will last longer than one day's news.
sawal: How many schools for one bomber? Who will keep that account?
ref: May 1968, France
A movement that began with a student revolt in Paris, in which a strike by close to ten million workers shut the country down and shook President de Gaulle's government.
Soweto uprising (1976)
School students in South Africa marched against apartheid education and the forcing of the Afrikaans language on them; hundreds were killed in police firing.
ank: student and youth groups called the strike
countries with walkouts from classes at the same time

h: Delhi's toxic air: plenty of plans, nobody accountable
dek: In ThePrint, Disha Sharma writes that Beijing cut its pollution by nearly 70 per cent in 12 years because every task there had one officer in charge, and this is the lesson Delhi needs to learn.
body: On 8 November Delhi's average AQI was 376, and by 10 at night 20 of the 59 monitoring stations had reached the 'severe' category. Environmentalists called it a health emergency, but no formal declaration came. Disha Sharma, who teaches at IIM Mumbai, argues that Delhi has no shortage of plans. What it lacks is anyone being held accountable when they fail.

There was the action plan in April, the Winter Action Plan from 1 November, and the Rs 8,300 crore 'Clean Air, Healthy Delhi' programme announced in July, 65 per cent of which will be paid by the World Bank. Even so, Delhi's annual PM2.5 level is stuck at around 100 micrograms per cubic metre. In Beijing, meanwhile, it fell from 89.5 in 2013 to 27 in 2025, and days of heavy pollution dropped from 58 to one.

According to the writer, Beijing's secret was not just clean fuel. Every task had a lead department and a named officer, districts were checked every month, and in 2016-17 central inspections across China held more than 17,000 officials responsible. The data was taken out of the hands of local officers and given to an independent body.

Delhi, by contrast, has many agencies, and key decisions such as land rest with the Centre, so everyone shifts the blame onto someone else. In 2024 the Supreme Court also asked why the air quality commission had not used Section 14 of its own law against officers who ignored its orders. The writer recommends making the chief secretary responsible for the clean air target, giving every task one department and a budget, publishing a scorecard every month, auditing the data independently, and drawing up a shared agreement among the states for the whole NCR.
nazar: Toxic air hits hardest those who cannot put an air purifier in their homes: labourers who work on the streets, rickshaw drivers, street vendors and children in the slums. Every year there is a debate about stubble burning, and every year the matter is put off until the next winter.

China's model cannot be copied as it is in a democracy, but the principle of accountability should matter even more in a democracy. Until some officer's or minister's job is tied to the quality of the air, the plans will go on breathing only on paper.
sawal: China held 17,000 officials accountable. How many has Delhi?
ref: PM2.5
Particles floating in the air smaller than 2.5 micrometres, which reach the lungs and the blood; the World Health Organization puts their safe annual limit at 5 micrograms per cubic metre.
Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM)
A statutory commission set up in 2021 that can issue orders to control pollution in Delhi-NCR and the nearby states, and can act against those who do not comply.
photo_note: The Houses of Parliament in the fog, Claude Monet

h: Sonia Gandhi's memoir: open about her private life, a curtain over politics
dek: In Newslaundry, Ashutosh Bhardwaj writes that 'Belonging' is a touching account of a young woman's life, but when it comes to politics it turns from self-examination into a defence of the family.
body: Writer and journalist Ashutosh Bhardwaj begins his review on the shore of Lake Como in Italy, where framed pictures of Mussolini were being sold near the spot where he was killed. In his view, unlike Germany, many Italians have never been able to look their fascist past in the eye. He sees the same silence in Sonia Gandhi's memoir 'Belonging: A Journey of Love'.

In the book Sonia remembers her father, Stefano Maino, as a generous man who served in the Italian army during the fascist regime and was much loved by his comrades. Bhardwaj's complaint is that the book is silent on whether Mussolini's military campaigns cast any shadow on that life. A writer who writes sharply about the dangers of right-wing politics in India shies away from the politics of the country where she was born.

The reviewer is even harder on the political part. The book presents Indira Gandhi's entry into politics as if she were a reluctant saviour who came to bring the Congress back to its socialist and secular ideals, not a ruthless politician. There is sympathy for Indira's short spell in Tihar during the Janata government, but no mention of the ordinary citizens jailed during the Emergency, and Sanjay Gandhi gets praise after a mild scolding.

Bhardwaj also grants the book its strengths: the writer's patience through years of attacks, and the love story of an Italian girl and an Indian young man in England. But in his view the book splits into two parts. The personal part is moving and the political part is mostly contrived. Citing Orwell's 'Shooting an Elephant', he says an apology was not necessary, but an examination of the political decisions of her mother-in-law, husband and son was, and an autobiography without self-examination loses its moral weight.
nazar: The memoirs of people who were close to power become the raw material of history, so their silences matter too. If the story of those jailed in the Emergency, those who suffered forced sterilisation and the poor whose homes were razed finds no place in a book by the most powerful family of that time, the gap is not just a literary one.
Today, when the current government is accused of Emergency-like excesses, the opposition's moral strength rests on settling the account of its own past with the same honesty.
sawal: What do the pictures of Mussolini sold at Lake Como remind us of?
ref: The Emergency (1975-77)
Indira Gandhi's government imposed the Emergency on 25 June 1975; civil rights were suspended, opposition leaders were jailed, the press was censored and a forced sterilisation drive was carried out.
Shooting an Elephant
George Orwell's 1936 essay in which, through the story of an English police officer in Burma who shoots an elephant under pressure from a crowd, he examines the hollowness of imperial power.

h: Children will pay the heaviest price for the failure at Antalya
dek: A coalition working on children's environmental rights says COP31, which ended without agreement, left children on their own on every front: fossil fuels, finance and climate education.
body: COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, ended without any shared decision. CERI, a coalition of groups working on children's environmental rights, whose statement CRIN has published as a commentary, has called this outcome unacceptable. According to it, the conference could neither build on earlier decisions nor reach agreement on the main 'cover decision'.

The coalition says that in the final draft the language on climate finance and on moving away from fossil fuels was either weakened or missing. In its place there was an emphasis on technologies such as carbon capture and pulling carbon out of the air, which the group sees as false solutions because they keep the world tied to the same oil and gas industry. Several countries also tried to roll back language on human rights and gender equality that had already been agreed.

The stakes are not small. According to the statement, the world is now clearly crossing the 1.5 degree limit, and a 2026 UNICEF report estimates that about 1.1 billion children live with at least three climate hazards, which strike directly at their health, education and safety.

Talks on a just transition were also pushed to next year. The coalition says the draft neither said which industries would close and what would replace them, nor gave any mechanism for children and vulnerable groups to take part. In that case, even new renewable energy industries could repeat the old story of displacement and pollution.

The bitterest episode concerns the 2027-2031 action plan on climate education. After two weeks of talks, a nearly finished text was rejected at the last minute by a single country, even though it spoke of making schools stronger against climate risks. The group wants countries to take these steps at home on their own, and wants the failure of this conference, which was called 'the COP of implementation', to be remembered until the next round of talks.
nazar: In India, it is children who carry the heaviest burden of heatwaves, floods and toxic air: schools close, studies are interrupted, lungs grow weak. The failure at Antalya means this burden will grow, while rich countries and oil states keep dodging their responsibility on finance.

In a system where one country's 'no' can wash away two weeks of work, questions about its rules are bound to come up. In the next round India should speak not only for its own interests but also for the children who have no seat at the table.
sawal: The safety of 1.1 billion children, left to one country's veto?
ref: Cover decision
The main political document of a climate conference, which sets the direction for the year. This time there was no agreement on it at all.
Carbon capture (CCUS)
Technology that catches carbon dioxide from factory smoke and buries it underground. Critics say it becomes an excuse to keep burning fossil fuels.

h: In Netanyahu's words, the same fire that came before Rabin's murder
dek: Yossi Mekelberg of Chatham House charges that after Arab parties grew stronger in the election, Netanyahu's incitement has brought Israel to the edge of political violence.
body: Arab parties did well in Israel's general election last month, and since then the writer finds Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's attitude racist. The charge is that Netanyahu called all 19 MPs who represent citizens of Palestinian origin supporters of terror, and almost branded as traitors the Jewish parties willing to work with them.

Mekelberg lists how this escalated: coded language during the campaign, a warning on polling day about the number of Arab voters, then the story of a 'stolen election', and in the new parliament the charge that Gadi Eisenkot, who has been asked to form a government, wants to join hands with parties that want to wipe out the Jewish state. Yet this same Netanyahu was once ready to take Mansour Abbas's Ra'am party into government.

The writer hears an echo of 1995 in this. After the Oslo Accords, hardline religious rabbis issued a 'din rodef' ruling against Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin, and the killer, Yigal Amir, cited it. According to the writer, Netanyahu, then leader of the opposition, was at the Jerusalem rally where Rabin was shown in a Nazi uniform, and he never apologised.

Today his ally is Itamar Ben-Gvir, who has been convicted of inciting racism and supporting a terrorist organisation, and who once made threats while showing off an emblem stolen from Rabin's car. The writer says the gap between the two is now as thin as paper, and that it is the fear of losing power that makes Netanyahu, caught up in a corruption trial, speak this way.

His warning is that this incitement could push some lone extremist to attack an Arab MP or a Jewish leader standing with them, and could stir up communal violence against Arab citizens. In the writer's view, Israel is on the brink of political violence, and much of the responsibility lies with Netanyahu.
nazar: Politics that calls the elected representatives of minorities 'enemies of the nation' and those who sit with them traitors is not unfamiliar to readers in India. Casting suspicion on a whole community's vote out of fear of defeat strikes at the root of democracy.
Rabin's murder shows that the language of hate never stays just language. Leaders who light such a fire cannot later wash their hands of its flames.
sawal: How quickly did Israel forget that rally with the Nazi uniform?
ref: Din rodef
An idea in Jewish religious law under which killing a person is justified by treating them as a threat to others' lives. Rabin's killer used it as his cover.
Oslo Accords
Agreements signed in 1993-95 between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization, which began Palestinian self-rule. Rabin was their main face.

h: Why Gen Z is on the streets: fees, rent and disappearing jobs
dek: According to Oscar Berglund of the University of Bristol, decades of neoliberal policy and the inflation since the pandemic lie at the root of youth movements around the world.
body: Oscar Berglund, who researches protest at the University of Bristol, does not see the 'Gen Z' movements that took to the streets of many countries in 2026 as just generational anger. Citing a new six-country survey by the Global Fund for a New Economy, he says their real cause is the rising cost of living since the pandemic, made worse by Trump's war with Iran and oil prices.

The writer puts this in a longer history. The neoliberal policies of the eighties and nineties hollowed out the welfare state, and after the 2008 crisis the cuts in Europe loaded the burden onto ordinary people and rescued the rich. When interest rates rose after the pandemic, the cost of living crisis came fully into the open.

In his view, young people are being hit on three fronts. In education, cuts in France sparked protests, and in Britain heavy fees and high-interest loans tie students down for decades. In jobs, unchecked AI is eating up entry-level work, and the writer links the protests in India to this same shrinking of chances too. In housing, each generation is pouring more of its income than the last into rent and instalments, and buying a home now depends on family wealth.

Berglund also points to the growing power of tech billionaires, whose data centres are swallowing water, electricity and jobs. He says those in power want the anger to fall on migrants, but protesters are now putting the blame on these very billionaires and on governments that dodge the root problem.

The writer also sees some signs of hope: strong support in the survey for taxing billionaires, the defeat in the US midterm elections of the candidates most favoured by tech billionaires, and a law protecting tenants in Spain after a general strike on housing. His advice is to keep up the pressure both at the ballot box and on the street.
nazar: For young Indians this picture is not foreign: leaked recruitment exam papers, contract jobs, expensive coaching and wild rents in the cities. The only difference is that here the anger is often turned towards religion and identity.
The Spanish example shows that organised pressure can change laws. The question is when the restlessness of our young people will turn into concrete demands on jobs and housing.
sawal: In Spain a strike produced a law. Where is India's youth anger heading?
ref: Neoliberalism
An economic outlook of cutting government spending, privatisation and giving the market a free hand, which spread around the world from the 1980s.
Indignados
A youth movement in Spain in 2011 that camped out in public squares against spending cuts and unemployment.

h: War in the hands of machines, and a last plea for diplomacy
dek: Former Pakistani foreign secretary Aizaz Ahmad Chaudhry argues that the way to protect ourselves from hybrid war fought with drones, AI and cyber attacks is a new global pact on 'indivisible security'.
body: Former Pakistani foreign secretary Aizaz Ahmad Chaudhry says the old face of war, with masses of soldiers, columns of tanks and fixed front lines, is now history. Last year's India-Pakistan clash and this year's US-Iran war are proof of it. Today's fighting is hybrid: cyber attacks, economic pressure and psychological war on social media, all at once.

Technology is at the centre of this change. According to the writer, missiles and armed drones allow strikes from far away that are fast and precise, and he claims that last year Pakistan shot down several Indian aircraft with missiles while they were flying far beyond visual range. In the Iran war too, most of the fighting was done with missiles guided by satellite and infrared. AI drones, loitering munitions and drone swarms have already arrived on the battlefield.

The writer believes this will take war further out of human control. Autonomous weapons do not understand the context of a situation and cannot show mercy, so the risk of war crimes rises and accountability blurs. Their speed could also send a conflict out of control. He cites Trump's threat to wipe out Iran's power grid, its bridges and even its 'civilisation' as an example of trying to break an enemy's morale through economic damage.

He links this to a world where power has the final say. Big powers are using force illegally, one-sidedly and without limit, and the UN Charter's promise of sovereignty is no longer kept. So middle and small countries are moving towards self-reliance, alliances with like-minded states, and investment in their own military technology and communication systems.

The writer's remedy is strong diplomacy: a new global pact on 'indivisible security', along the lines of the UN Charter, binding every country to respect one another's sovereignty and borders. In his eyes this is the way to avert the destruction ahead.
nazar: The claim about Indian aircraft comes from the Pakistani side, and India gives a different account of that clash. But the article's larger worry applies on both sides of the border: two nuclear neighbours have entered a race in drones and AI, and the price is paid out of the budgets for schools, hospitals and jobs.

The day a machine fires without a human decision, the question of accountability will be the first to die. India and Pakistan should stand together in the demand for an international ban on autonomous weapons, not in a race.
sawal: If a machine fires on its own, who is guilty of the war crime?
ref: Hybrid war
Fighting in which military attacks are combined with weapons such as cyber attacks, economic sanctions, propaganda and social pressure, all used at once.
Loitering munition
A drone-like weapon that hovers over a target for a long time and, when it gets the chance, crashes into it and explodes.

h: Twenty people stuck at the border for two days, and nobody will take them
dek: About twenty people, including women and children, are stuck in no man's land on the border next to Assam's Sribhumi district, and Bangladesh alleges they were pushed across in the middle of the night.
body: About twenty people, including women and children, are reported to have been stuck for two days on the empty land between Madanpur in Assam's Sribhumi district and Latu Pallathal in Bangladesh's Barlekha area. Officials on both sides are not letting them into their territory. Maktoob reported this citing reports in The Times of India and the Bangladeshi newspaper The Daily Star.

According to The Daily Star, Border Guard Bangladesh on Thursday night blocked an alleged attempt by the BSF to push these twenty people across the border at Moulvibazar. A video is also circulating on social media that appears to show Bangladeshi guards stopping a group, including women, in the dark of night. In Meherpur, an attempt to send four more people across in the same way was foiled.

A day earlier, Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma had posted on X that 38 'illegal infiltrators' had been sent out of Assam in the early hours, along with a picture of women and children. Maktoob says it could not independently confirm any link between the two incidents.

A 'pushback' means pushing people across the border without any formal deportation or handover process. In July, Sarma himself told the Assembly that of the 31,789 people sent back over forty years, 29,663 were 'pushbacks', and only 470 were formally deported.
nazar: In a state whose own figures show formal deportations are not even two in a hundred, the 'pushback' is not an exception, it is the policy. No hearing, no court, no talks with the other country, just driving people towards the border at night. If there is doubt about someone's citizenship, the law should decide it; leaving children in the cold in no man's land is not justified under any law.
sawal: Whose government is responsible for the children stuck in no man's land?
ref: Pushback
Pushing people across the border without a court order or a formal handover to the other country. Human rights groups see it as arbitrary and inhuman.
No man's land
The strip between two countries' border posts for which, in practice, neither country accepts responsibility.

h: Amrit Wilson's OCI card: charged with 'anti-India' activity, no details given
dek: The Delhi High Court said the order cancelling the UK-based writer's OCI card gives no details at all of the activities she was accused of.
body: Writer, journalist and activist Amrit Wilson was born in India and went to Britain to study in 1961. She took a British passport in 2009, got a PIO card in 2014 and an OCI card in December 2017. In November 2022 the government sent her a notice saying she was engaged in 'harmful propaganda' against the Indian government and 'anti-India activities', and asked for a reply within fifteen days.

Wilson denied the charges and said no specific allegations had been given, and that the material behind the notice should be shown to her. There was no reply for three months, and on 17 March 2023 her card was cancelled under Section 7D(e) of the Citizenship Act. Even in court, the government gave no reasons in its affidavit and said the material could only be given in a sealed cover.

Justice Amit Mahajan held that neither the notice nor the order mentioned any particular activity, so Wilson never got a chance to defend herself and natural justice was not followed. The court told the government to issue a fresh notice with concrete reasons within a week. If the whole matter cannot be disclosed, a summary of the material should be given with the sensitive parts removed, or she should be allowed to see it. Wilson will reply within a week, and a fresh order will come within two weeks after that. Until then, for four weeks at most, the old order will stay in force.
nazar: 'Anti-India' has become a label that can be stuck on someone without evidence, or even without spelling out the charge. The OCI cards of critical writers and journalists are being cancelled one by one, and the sealed cover has become the answer to every question. The court only reminded the government that a person who is accused must know the accusation, and even this basic point the government had to hear from a court.
sawal: How can anyone answer charges that were never written down?
ref: OCI card
Overseas Citizen of India: a status given to people of Indian origin who have taken foreign citizenship, which lets them come to, travel in and live in India without a visa.
Sealed cover
A practice in which the government shows its material only to the judge and not to the other side. The Supreme Court has said many times that it goes against a fair hearing.

h: Rampur: 18 police calls to Sharif's home on the day he was killed
dek: Mohammad Sharif Khan, acquitted after eighteen years in jail, was shot dead a few hours after a police verification, and his family is questioning the role of the police.
body: Mohammad Sharif Khan, 53, of Rampur, was an accused in the 2007 CRPF camp attack case. In October 2025 the Allahabad High Court acquitted him and four others, and in November 2025 he walked out of Bareilly jail after nearly eighteen years. On 10 November 2026, two masked men shot him in Khajuria village. He was reportedly hit by sixteen bullets.

According to The Wire, the police called the family 18 times that same day. His brother Shaheen Khan says a constable named Bunty called him 11 times, and seven calls went to his sister-in-law. Sharif had no phone. He went to the police station and waited an hour and a half, but found neither the constable nor the station officer. On his way back, about five hundred metres from the station, he was killed in front of his son, Abu Baiz.

The son's complaint names station officer Manoj Kumar Pandey and constable Bunty, but the FIR names only Bunty. The family alleges that the police stopped them from taking him to a private hospital and that more than two hours were lost. The family is asking for a CBI inquiry. Gulab Khan, a relative acquitted in the same case, was called by Bareilly police for verification on 15 November, but he did not go for fear of his life. The police say the investigation is on and that keeping watch on acquitted people is routine.
nazar: A man the court found innocent was made a target again by the police in the name of 'surveillance'. Whether this string of phone calls was a coincidence or someone was being told where he would be is the family's question, and it cannot be answered by the same police whose men are named in the complaint. Without an independent inquiry, this case too will join those deaths whose files are never closed, only forgotten.
sawal: Why is the station officer named in the complaint missing from the FIR?
ref: Police verification
Regular attendance and questioning at the police station for people released from jail or linked to a case. According to lawyers, it has become a tool of harassment for acquitted Muslims.

h: Writer Ravi Hanj arrested at the airport over a book on Basavanna
dek: Karnataka police stopped the Chicago-based Kannada writer at Kochi airport and arrested him, and the state government has already decided to seize copies of the book.
body: Chicago-based Kannada writer Ravi Hanj was stopped at Kochi International Airport on Saturday, 21 November, as he was leaving the country. A look out circular had been issued against him. He was brought to Bengaluru and arrested. There are complaints against him in several places, including Belagavi. The report does not say under which sections the case has been registered.

The controversy is over his six-hundred-page book 'Basava Mantapa', which is accused of twisting the teachings of Basavanna, the twelfth-century social reformer. Hanj has written that Veerashaiva and Lingayat are one tradition and that there are contradictions in Sharana literature (the writings of Basavanna's movement). Copies of the book were torn and burnt in Karnataka and Maharashtra. Hanj later apologised, saying his words had been misunderstood, but the Basava Samiti rejected the apology.

The state cabinet has approved seizing the book and taking legal action against the writer and the publisher, Vishweshwar Bhat, editor of Vishwavani. Chief Minister DK Shivakumar warned that writing that 'disturbs public order' would be acted upon. Along with Congress ministers, BJP leaders such as Yediyurappa and BY Vijayendra also joined the demand for action. Minister Eshwar Khandre said the Centre would be asked in writing to get Hanj's videos taken down.
nazar: The answer to disagreeing with a book is another book, and in this very dispute such a reply was already published in 2025. But here the ruling party and the opposition are speaking with one voice, getting the writer picked up at an airport and his book seized. Basavanna himself argued against orthodoxy; shutting the door on debate in his name is the most backward use of his legacy.
sawal: After the writer apologised, what did the arrest achieve?
ref: Look out circular
A notice from the police or an investigating agency under which a person can be stopped at an airport or border so that they do not leave the country.
Lingayat-Veerashaiva debate
An old dispute in Karnataka over whether Lingayats are a separate religion or part of the Veerashaiva tradition. In 2018 the state government recommended minority status for Lingayats.

h: 'Not calling it arrest does not make detention lawful': women journalists' body
dek: Replying to Delhi Police's affidavit in the Supreme Court, the Network of Women in Media said the right to gather news does not depend on any government accreditation.
body: During the protests in Delhi in October against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, journalists were removed from the spot, made to sit in police vehicles and stopped from moving about. Last week Delhi Police told the Supreme Court that this was crowd control and 'removal for verification', not detention or arrest, and that there was no deliberate interference in the journalists' work.

In its reply filed on Saturday, the Network of Women in Media, India said the police cannot justify restricting someone's freedom just by changing the words. The police had argued that the Supreme Court's direction of 11 October, which said the work of journalists, lawyers and other professionals must not be obstructed, does not apply to 'reel makers' and influencers. The group said the right to gather news does not rest on accreditation, a job or an office ID card, and the same holds for freelance and digital journalists.

Three women journalists had complained of sexual harassment by policemen. The police said the allegations were not confirmed, nothing showed up on CCTV, and the complaints were closed. The group says it is wrong to have the inquiry done by the same force whose men are accused, there should be an independent inquiry, and a complainant not pursuing the matter does not prove the incident never happened.
nazar: If we accept the police definition, even keeping someone shut in a vehicle for hours is not detention, just 'removal'. And now the police also want to decide who is a journalist. The ruling in this case will decide whether anyone can photograph a crowd on the street questioning those in power.
sawal: Why should the police decide who is a journalist?
ref: Network of Women in Media, India
A nationwide group of women working in the media, which raises issues of journalists' safety and working conditions.

h: Families driven out of Darfur, Khartoum's winter and shrinking aid
dek: Displaced families settled in Al-Ghadir in Omdurman are sleeping on the ground without blankets, while not even half the money for Sudan's relief plan has come in.
body: Fatima Mohammed Haroun, about sixty, was driven out of West Darfur as soon as the war began in 2023. A year ago her son went missing and her daughter-in-law died after giving birth, and now she alone looks after four grandchildren. The family lives in a crumbling mud building in Al-Ghadir, north of Omdurman, and has received no relief since being displaced. Being close to the hills, the nights here are very cold, and people sleep on the ground without blankets.

Khaira Matar Hassan's husband went to look for work in the gold mines of Chad in 2023 and was never heard from again. She raises seven children by washing and ironing clothes, in a broken house covered with plastic and cloth. She too has received nothing from the government or any agency.

The war between the army and the paramilitary RSF, going on since April 2023, has driven more than 8.5 million people in Sudan from their homes, with 414,252 displaced in Khartoum state alone. According to the International Organization for Migration and the UN refugee agency, 15.4 million people need emergency shelter, but the money is enough to help only ten per cent. Not even half the amount for the 2026 relief plan of $2.9 billion has come in. An official of the Darfur regional government admitted that there is a winter plan, but resources are short.
nazar: The world's biggest displacement tragedy sits at the margins of the news, and the aid purse is shrinking just as fast. Weapons for the war arrive from somewhere or other, but there is no money for blankets. Women like Fatima and Khaira are telling us that this winter will turn deadly not because of the weather, but because of the world's indifference.
sawal: There is money for weapons, so why not for blankets?
ref: RSF
Rapid Support Forces: Sudan's paramilitary force, which has been fighting the army since April 2023 and is accused of large-scale violence in Darfur.

h: Adi groups of the Siang valley hand Amit Shah four demands
dek: The Home Minister, in Itanagar, promised talks and a rehabilitation package, but the groups opposing the dam are holding firm on stopping the survey and freeing those in custody.
ask: Stop the pre-feasibility work, free those detained, withdraw the security forces
body: In Arunachal Pradesh, opponents of the 11,200 megawatt Siang Upper Multipurpose Project put their demands directly to Union Home Minister Amit Shah during his visit. On Friday, Adi Bane Kebang United, a body that represents the Adi community, and the Siang Indigenous Farmers' Forum handed over a joint memorandum. It makes four points: all pre-feasibility work should stop at once, detained protesters should be released, security forces should be pulled out of the valley, and there should be a judicial inquiry into the violence of 23 October.

On Saturday, at a ceremony in Itanagar to present the President's Colour to the state police, Shah said he had come himself to clear people's fears. According to him, every decision on the dam will be taken with local people on board, their culture and traditions will be protected, and those affected will get the best rehabilitation package in the country. He asked the protesters to talk to the Home Ministry through the state government.

In October, after four people were hurt by tear gas in East Siang, a 12-hour bandh (shutdown) was called, followed by arson and vandalism in Pasighat. People fear the dam will uproot villages, drown ancestral land and damage the fragile hill environment. At the time of writing, the groups had not responded to Shah's remarks.
nazar: The Home Minister speaks of dialogue while companies of central forces are posted in the valley and people from the movement are in jail. Talks will be believable only when the survey stops and the detainees are freed. Decide first and seek consent later: unless that order is reversed, the Adi community's distrust will not ease.
sawal: How can the table for talks be laid while comrades are still in jail?
ref: Adi Bane Kebang
A body rooted in the tradition of the Adi community's customary apex council. The Adi villages of the Siang valley would be the worst hit by the dam.

h: Ramanathapuram's fishers ask for a bank and a panchayat of their own
dek: On World Fisheries Day, hundreds of fishermen and fisherwomen gathered near the district collectorate, and a separate rally was held in Thangachimadam.
ask: A cooperative bank for fishers, a separate panchayat, our place on the coastal map
body: In Ramanathapuram, Tamil Nadu, hundreds of fishermen and fisherwomen from villages across the district gathered near the district collectorate on 21 November, World Fisheries Day. The protest by the Ramanathapuram District Fishermen's Association was led by its president Balasamy, and secretary Anand addressed the gathering.

The association put five demands to the state government. The age limit for cooperative relief schemes should be raised from 60 to 75 years. Like farmers, fishers should have a separate cooperative bank that lends at low interest. Fishing villages should be grouped into a panchayat (local council) of the community's own. The coastal zone management map should clearly record the traditional places for parking boats, weaving nets, repairing boats and fishing. And the 1991 Coastal Regulation Zone notification should be strictly enforced without any amendment.

The same day, in Thangachimadam on Rameswaram island, a fishermen's association held a rally from St Teresa's Church to RK Lion Mahal with the slogan of protecting fishers' lives and property, led by Irudaya Mary. Members of a fisherwomen's organisation also took part. The report does not mention any response from the government to the demands.
nazar: The demand to mark fishers' places on the coastal map is really a fight over land. With the shoreline being sold off so fast for ports, tourism and industry, not being on paper becomes the first step to eviction. That fear is why they insist on the 1991 notification.
sawal: Why does the map not show where nets are woven?
ref: Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ)
The 1991 notification that restricts construction and industry near the seashore. Later amendments loosened many of its curbs, which fishers' groups oppose.

h: Health care stalls in 650 Ferozepur villages as mission staff strike
dek: A Punjab-wide strike over regularisation has hit the district's 92 Ayushman Arogya health centres.
ask: Regularisation with pay protection, or equal pay for equal work
body: In Punjab's Ferozepur district, about 350 employees of the National Health Mission have been on an indefinite strike for nearly two weeks. It is part of a movement running in every district of the state on the call of the National Health Mission Employees Union (Punjab). The strikers include community health officers, auxiliary nurse midwives, staff nurses, RBSK teams, Ayurvedic medical officers, pharmacy officers, the TB department, lab technicians and office staff.

Services have broken down in about 650 villages of this district of around eight lakh (800,000) people. At 92 Ayushman Arogya centres, OPD and treatment for blood pressure, diabetes and infections have been hit. Screening for non-communicable diseases and TB has stopped, and the district laboratory cannot run ELISA tests for dengue and chikungunya. Services at 853 schools and 1,206 anganwadi (village childcare) centres, vaccination and check-ups of pregnant women are also reported to be affected.

The union wants jobs regularised with pay protection, or equal pay for equal work. Its leaders say that Aam Aadmi Party leaders now in power came to these same protests under the previous government and promised regularisation. The union has warned that the movement will intensify if there are no talks. The report carries no response from the government.
nazar: The real sickness is keeping on contract, for years, the very workers who carry a village's entire primary health system on their shoulders. Promises made in opposition and forgotten in power: Punjab is repeating the same story that plays out with scheme workers in every state.
sawal: How costly will locked laboratories be in dengue season?
ref: National Health Mission
A centrally sponsored scheme that runs health services in villages and cities. Most of its staff are on contract and have long demanded regularisation.

h: Yamunanagar cane farmers dig in; Saraswati mill idle for five days
dek: Demanding 600 rupees a quintal, BKU farmers have pitched tents outside Agriculture Minister Shyam Singh Rana's house in Radaur.
ask: Raise the cane price to 600 rupees a quintal
body: In Yamunanagar, Haryana, the crushing season at Saraswati Sugar Mill began five days ago, but not a single trolley of cane has reached the mill yet. Because of the farmers' agitation, the mill's machines are standing still. Farmers are refusing to supply cane at the price fixed by the government.

Led by Subhash Gurjar, district president of the Bharatiya Kisan Union (Charuni), farmers reached Agriculture Minister Shyam Singh Rana's residence in Radaur, set up tents and began an indefinite sit-in. The BKU's Ratanman faction has also joined, widening the movement. Farmers from different blocks have been given day and night shifts so the sit-in keeps going without a break.

Saturday's sit-in was chaired by district general secretary Gurveer Singh. Gurjar said the protest will continue until the cane price is 600 rupees a quintal. The farmers have asked the government for a quick decision and said that if none comes, they will meet and decide their next step. The report records no response from the mill management or the government.
nazar: Tents outside the minister's house and silence outside the mill say the same thing: costs have gone up and prices have not kept pace. With crushing stopped, both the mill and the farmers lose, so the longer the government delays, the more the standing cane will dry in the fields.
sawal: Whose books will carry the loss of the cane left standing in the fields?
ref: State Advised Price (SAP)
The cane price set by a state government above the Centre's minimum price, which mills pay farmers. It sparks protests every year in Haryana and Punjab.

h: Chitehra mahapanchayat: no garbage dump next to our homes
dek: Villagers protesting the Dadri municipal council's garbage depot gave the administration a month, and announced they will gather again on 20 December.
ask: Shut the garbage depot at once and move it away from where people live
body: In Chitehra village of Gautam Buddh Nagar, villagers held a mahapanchayat on Sunday to oppose a garbage depot being built by the Dadri municipal council. The depot is coming up close to the homes of Chitehra and Nayi Basti. The villagers want it shut immediately and the garbage disposed of at a suitable place away from homes.

The mahapanchayat was chaired by Jairam Bhagat and conducted by Samajwadi Party leader Vachan Bhati. Balraj Singh, national president of the Bharatiya Kisan Union (Balraj), said the depot would spread filth and raise the risk of disease, but officials do not care about the villagers' health. Vachan Bhati accused the municipal council of acting arbitrarily and said children, the elderly and nearby families would suffer the most. Farmer leader Hemu Gurjar also demanded that the depot be removed at once.

The villagers handed a memorandum at Dadri police station and gave the administration a month. They announced that if the depot is not shut, another mahapanchayat will be held on 20 December and they will fight it out to the end. The report carries no word from the municipal council or the administration.
nazar: NCR cities often dump their garbage on the very villages whose land has already gone to urbanisation. If the choice of where to put a dump is made without asking the village, every new site will see a mahapanchayat just like this.
sawal: Who asked the village when the site for the garbage depot was chosen?
ref: Mahapanchayat
A large gathering of many villages or communities, an old way of making collective decisions and running movements in western Uttar Pradesh and Haryana.

h: Pratappur blocks the road for hours over elephants, rations and power bills
dek: In Surajpur district, hundreds of villagers led by farmer leader Shivbhajan Singh Maravi blocked the road at Chowk No. 11.
ask: Protect lives and property from elephants, stop ration cuts, cheaper electricity
body: In Pratappur, in Chhattisgarh's Surajpur district, villagers' anger over repeated attacks by wild elephants and a host of farming troubles spilled onto the road. Led by farmer leader Shivbhajan Singh Maravi, hundreds of farmers and villagers gathered at Chowk No. 11 and blocked traffic for several hours.

The villagers say elephant attacks in the Pratappur forest range have taken lives and destroyed crops, but the administration has made no effective arrangements. The movement put forward four demands. First, concrete steps to protect people's lives and crops from wild elephants. Second, an end to the cuts in rations for poor families. Third, correction of errors in the recorded paddy area of farmers, so they can sell their full harvest. Fourth, a check on steadily rising electricity bills.

The protesters handed a memorandum addressed to the Governor and the administration to the tehsildar (local revenue officer), seeking quick decisions on all four demands and relief for those affected. The report mentions no response from officials, the police or the forest department.
nazar: At the root of the human-elephant conflict in the Surguja division lie the felling of forests and mining, which have broken the elephants' corridors. In the same region, cuts in rations and recorded paddy area are a double blow for poor Adivasi (indigenous) farmers. The four demands look separate, but they all ask one question: who is responsible for protecting a village's livelihood?
sawal: What will a paddy area shrunk on paper take away from the farmer?
ref: Paddy area (rakba)
The area of a farmer's registered paddy fields. Government procurement in Chhattisgarh is based on it, so if the area is recorded as smaller, the farmer cannot sell the full harvest.

h: Colombia changes government, and the Amazon loses its shield
dek: On Democracy Now!, former Colombian environment official Irene Vélez-Torres explains how the new right-wing government has pulled back from both the push to quit fossil fuels and the protection of the Amazon.
by: Amy Goodman (in conversation with Irene Vélez-Torres)
body: The UN climate summit COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, was in its final days when the independent American news programme Democracy Now! broadcast this conversation from there. Host Amy Goodman opens with something jarring: the biggest cause of the planet's heating, namely coal, oil and gas, is almost missing from the official negotiating table.

Her guest is Irene Vélez-Torres, who was Colombia's minister of mines and energy in President Gustavo Petro's government and then acting minister of the environment. Together with the Netherlands she led the Santa Marta conference, where seven months ago more than fifty countries came together intending to phase out fossil fuels.

Vélez-Torres says the coalition now has 57 governments, and it also includes civil society groups, provincial governments and lawmakers. UN negotiations run by consensus, so even one or two countries can block the way. That is why a parallel forum was set up. According to her, about eighty per cent of the world's emissions are linked to fossil fuels, yet their production is hardly discussed, and she blames the lobby of oil and gas companies for this.

The coalition is working on three fronts: a roadmap for every country to exit fossil fuels, decarbonising the trade of countries that sell oil and coal, and a change in the financial system so that countries of the Global South can steer their economies in a new direction. The next conference is due in Tuvalu in July 2027. She calls the 'loss and damage' fund inadequate and full of paperwork hurdles.

Then the talk turns to Colombia. Petro's term ended in August, and right-wing President Abelardo de la Espriella took the country out of the Santa Marta coalition. According to Vélez-Torres, new agreements with the US on critical minerals and nuclear energy hurt Colombia's sovereignty, because they contain conditions such as US approval for mining projects and sharing information about underground resources.

The gravest charge concerns the Amazon. The Petro government had declared 42 per cent of the country's territory a zone free of fossil fuels. Vélez-Torres says the new government is reversing this protection, which will affect the water system of the whole region including Bogotá, and she calls it 'ecocide', the destruction of the environment. These are her claims, which the programme did not separately check. At the end there is a glimpse of a 'Make Polluters Pay' protest outside the summit, where people were demanding a bigger climate fund from rich countries.
nazar: This conversation shows how fragile climate policy is: a single election can undo years of work. Whether it is the Amazon or Hasdeo and Nicobar, when forest protection hangs on a government's whims, the Adivasis and farmers who live there are the first to pay the price.

For a coal-dependent country like India, the Santa Marta question is uncomfortable but necessary: how to build a way out, with money from rich polluters, without putting the burden of change on poor countries.
sawal: Why did the protection of forty-two per cent of the land collapse in one election?
ref: Santa Marta conference
A 2026 conference led by Colombia and the Netherlands, where more than fifty countries began work on a path to phase out fossil fuels.
COP31
The 31st annual conference of the parties to the UN climate treaty, being held this time in Antalya, Turkey.

h: Gold buried in a pit: the home that did not count its daughters
dek: The eleventh instalment of Neha Naruka's memoir series 'Mritatmaon ka Desh' recalls two dead women to ask whose passing makes a home weep.
body: Neha Naruka, the Vagishwari award-winning poet whose collection 'Phati Hatheliyan' (Cracked Palms) drew much attention, is writing a memoir series on Sammukh called 'Mritatmaon ka Desh' (Land of the Dead Souls). The eleventh instalment, 'Gaddhe Mein Sona' (Sona in the Pit), is not a poem, but its language comes very close to poetry.

The memory turns on two people. One is a sister-in-law who read Gulshan Nanda's novels while splitting lentils on the hand mill, and who died in a fire from a lantern. The other is Sona, a cousin just a year older than the writer, whose father died as soon as she was born, and who after her death was placed in a basket and buried somewhere unknown.

The writer records, in fine detail, the inequality inside a single home. She got her mother's milk and a cradle; Sona got buttermilk. When Sona died, someone expressed relief that there was no longer a wedding to worry about. The old family diary holds her date of birth and horoscope, but nowhere does it say who cried for her. According to the writer, such homes mourn only those who earn; a daughter is one more mouth, one more dowry.

In between comes a Sona of today too, a girl who works in a beauty parlour and is afraid of marriage and love because a friend of hers died within a year of her wedding. The writer advises her to keep working, but does not hide her own inner weariness.
At the end she imagines a pit she could lie down in to talk to Sona. A name that means gold, and an endless sleep in the earth: this irony hangs over the whole piece.
nazar: This piece speaks of the violence that never becomes news: a daughter buried without mourning. Behind the sex ratio figures lie countless unrecorded deaths like this, and literature is doing the work of giving them back their names.
sawal: The diary records the horoscope, so why not the tears?
ref: Mritatmaon ka Desh
Neha Naruka's ongoing memoir series on Sammukh, which remembers forgotten deaths in the family and the small town.

h: Kasturi: searching for the fragrance lost in her own name
dek: Dogri writer Krishna Prem's story 'Kasturi', in Yogita Yadav's Hindi translation, calls the girl buried inside a mother by her own name.
body: This time Sammukh's series of translated Dogri stories brings Krishna Prem's 'Kasturi' (Musk). Born in Shimla in 1948, Krishna Prem is a well-known voice of modern Dogri fiction. She was a newsreader at Radio Jammu and has published several collections, from 'Sur te Taal' to 'Kasturi'. The Hindi version is by Yogita Yadav, a fiction writer who won the Jnanpith Navlekhan award.

In her home and neighbourhood, the heroine is only 'Jagtu's mother'. She comes to a confidante she calls Bebu ji and says her son has become irritable and withdrawn, perhaps caught up with some girl. To get her to open up, the narrator calls her by her real name, Kasturi, and this small thing stirs something inside her.

Then the memories open up: the village well, the temple, the neem tree, and the boy from childhood who drew closer as they played. The two had pressed their palm prints in wet clay on the temple wall and made a childish promise. She was married elsewhere, the boy joined the army, and then there was no news of him. The image of grain being ground in the hand mill shows how a person gets ground down by compromises.

A few days later Kasturi comes back and says she went to that same wall. Between the faded palm prints there is now a phone number written in charcoal, as if today's love has become more direct. By the end of the story she understands that this fragrance was not given by anyone else; it is her own.
nazar: Linguistic diversity does not mean just counting dialects; it also means access to the stories of those languages. Stories like these, coming from Dogri into Hindi, show that the question of a woman's buried longings is the same in every tongue.
sawal: What does the charcoal number between the clay palms say?
ref: Dogri
The main language of the Jammu region, added to the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution in 2003.
Kasturi
Musk, the fragrance formed in the navel of the musk deer; in folk speech the image stands for something a person searches for outside but which lies within.

h: Sama Chakeva: Mithila's folk festival that burns the gossip's moustache
dek: Writing from his ancestral village, Ashutosh Kumar Thakur says Sama Chakeva is not just a game of clay toys but also women's collective court against rumour.
body: Ashutosh Kumar Thakur, a commentator and translator in English and Hindi, has returned after many years to Uren, his ancestral village on the India-Nepal border. In this essay published on Janaki Pul, he records the difference between the racing clock of the big city and the still time of the village through the smell of new paddy ears, the wet earth of the Brahmasthan (village shrine) and extinguished lamps.

As a child, he saw Sama Chakeva, which begins after Chhath, as just a game of clay toys. Now he sees in it a whole outlook of care for the environment and respect for women. The festival is not held in temples or closed rooms but on village paths, at crossroads and in fields, where girls and women gather with clay figurines in decorated bamboo baskets. Maithils on both sides of the border sing the same songs.

The story comes from the Puranas. A man named Chugla falsely accuses Sama, Krishna's daughter; Krishna, without checking, curses her to become a bird, and her husband Chakeva too becomes a bird to stay by her side. Her brother Samb, known in folk tradition as Satbhaiya, does penance and frees his sister from the curse.

According to the writer, the brother-sister bond in this festival is one of equality and trust, not just protection. In the rituals the gossip's moustache is burnt and the songs scold him, which means that every year the women of the village put the rumour-monger on trial. Welcoming the migratory birds coming down from the Himalayas is also part of it. In the moonlight of Kartik Purnima (the full moon of the month of Kartik) the figurines are bid farewell in the water and 'samdaun' songs are sung.
nazar: In an age when one false post is enough to destroy a woman's reputation, this folk festival that puts the gossip in the dock feels strangely modern. The songs shared across the border also remind us that lines on a map do not divide culture.
sawal: What will the gossip's burning moustache teach today's trolls?
ref: Sama Chakeva
A brother-sister folk festival of Mithila (the Terai region of Bihar and Nepal), celebrated from after Chhath until Kartik Purnima.
Samdaun
Maithili farewell songs, sung when a daughter leaves for her marital home and when the Sama Chakeva figurines are immersed.

h: Sooni Ghati ka Geet: Prabhat, Allahabad's forgotten poet
dek: In Hindwi's Bela, Avinash Mishra remembers the Prabhat (Prabhatranjan) who produced an important collection of Nayi Kavita at eighteen and then vanished into obscurity.
body: Avinash Mishra's essay begins with the memory of another poet who died young, Prakash, who took his own life in poverty and in whose name the 'Prakash Vritti' now publishes first collections. From there the writer comes to Prabhat, and makes clear that this is not the well-known poet Prabhat of today but a different poet from the Allahabad of the 1950s and 60s.

This Prabhat's only collection, 'Sooni Ghati ka Geet' (Song of the Lonely Valley), was published in 1959 by Sahitya Bhavan, Allahabad, when he was eighteen. The name on the book is Prabhatranjan, but everyone kept calling him Prabhat. Its preface is a statement in favour of Nayi Kavita (New Poetry), which says that perfection is a kind of death.

The essay builds his portrait with the help of Malayaj's diary, the memoirs of Doodhnath Singh and Gyanranjan, a poem by Neelabh, and 'Kuchh Ashke Jigar', a collection of letters edited by Priyamvad. According to Gyanranjan, it was Prabhat who introduced him to Neruda and European cinema. His relationship with his father, the critic Vishwambhar 'Manav', was bitter. This reader of Pound, Rimbaud and Ibn-e-Safi later had to go through shock treatment again and again. According to the writer, no firm date of his death is recorded; according to an old letter, he spent his last days at the cremation ground of Kakraha Ghat.

Turning to the poems, Mishra says this collection matters in the history of Nayi Kavita: nature, love, memory and modern unease, with experiments between song and free verse. He also notes that the woman in these poems is often defined only by her relation to the male speaker.
nazar: This essay points a finger at literary history's habit of remembering only successful names. Keeping count of how many talents mental illness and poverty swallowed is as important as counting awards.
sawal: In which history will the days spent in the cremation ground's pavilion be recorded?
ref: Nayi Kavita
The Hindi poetry movement of the 1950s that moved away from metre and idealism and put the ordinary person's experience and modern restlessness at the centre.
Malayaj
Hindi poet and critic (1935-1982), whose diaries are an important record of literary life in Allahabad.
photo_note: The last days of Shah Jahan

h: The ektara is silent: ten poems for Teejan Bai
dek: A poem series by art and music writer Rajendra Sharma, published on Samalochan, sees Teejan Bai's passing as the silent stage of Pandavani.
body: Samalochan has published a series of ten short poems by Rajendra Sharma in memory of Teejan Bai, the Pandavani singer from Chhattisgarh. Born in Saharanpur in 1966, Sharma has written more than three hundred articles on art and music in the last ten years, writes the 'Sabrang' column in 'Naya Gyanodaya' and edits the literature and arts page of a daily in Ranchi.

Each poem has its own title, such as 'Mahaprayan' (The Great Departure), 'Pandavani Ne Unhein Gaya' (Pandavani Sang Her), 'Ektara Chup Hai' (The Ektara Is Silent) and 'Chhattisgarh Rota Nahin' (Chhattisgarh Does Not Weep). These poems are not a biography and do not list the events of Teejan Bai's life. They reflect on what a great artist leaves behind.

A central idea of the series is that Teejan Bai did not sing Pandavani; Pandavani found its voice through her. After she is gone, characters of the Mahabharata such as Draupadi, Bhima and Karna seem to stand alone and voiceless. One poem places her ashes at the meeting of rivers, from where her voice dissolves into the folk.

Chhattisgarh's grief, too, makes no noise; it seeps into the fields, the crops and the folk songs. The poet himself reads the empty stage and the silent ektara (one-stringed instrument) as a kind of Pandavani that one has to listen to inwardly. In the end the pain of parting turns into gratitude, with the faith that the voice will live on in new women singers.
nazar: A woman from Chhattisgarh's Pardhi Adivasi community sang, in her own tongue and her own style, the epic that was long considered the right of only a few. To remember her is to remember the heritage of folk art that villages, more than institutions, have saved.
sawal: From whose throat will Draupadi's voice now rise?
ref: Pandavani
A folk singing style of Chhattisgarh in which a performer holding a tambura tells episodes of the Mahabharata through song, acting and dialogue.

h: An ode to Europe, with praise and a reckoning
dek: Scroll has published two poems by Ghayath Almadhoun from the anthology 'For Gaza: Art Against Genocide', which look at Europe and at loss through a refugee's eyes.
body: From the anthology 'For Gaza: Art Against Genocide', edited by Jeet Thayil and Pascal Berton and published by HarperCollins India, Scroll has printed two poems by the Palestinian poet Ghayath Almadhoun. The speaker of the poems was born a refugee in the Yarmouk camp in Damascus, calls Palestine his homeland and now lives in Europe. The page also carries a photograph of the shrouded body of a child killed in an air strike in Gaza.

The first poem, 'Ode to Sorrow', speaks directly to Europe, with both affection and irony. Through everyday things like taxes, erratic weather, dark winters and vitamin D deficiency, the speaker shows that Europeans and 'outsiders' are made of the same clay. To the question often asked about women in the Middle East, he replies by comparing the dates on which women in Syria and Switzerland got the right to vote.

Then, while praising Europe's art, music, philosophy and literature, the poem sets before it the account of colonialism, the slave trade, racism, fascism and the Holocaust. The speaker links his birth as a refugee to Europe's decisions on Palestine after the Second World War, and while thanking it for a passport and freedom, questions its double standards.

The second poem, 'Everything's the Same', is slow and personal: the memory of a beloved who is gone, an empty chair, the damp of a palm on the door handle, hair caught in a comb. Held together by a refrain, these images connect private grief to the larger devastation of exile and war.
nazar: This poem catches the hypocrisy that speaks the language of human rights while still treating some lives as worth less. For a South Asian reader, whose history too has passed through colonialism, this reckoning is not foreign.
sawal: How many illusions can one date for the right to vote shatter?
ref: Yarmouk camp
The largest settlement of Palestinian refugees, set up near Damascus in 1957, which was badly destroyed in the Syrian civil war.
